meta.title: Who really said "The time to be happy is now. The place to be happy is here. The way to be happy is to make others so"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's Robert G. Ingersoll. The three-part wording is documented in his 1899 phonograph recording; the thought closes his 1872 lecture “The Gods.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The time to be happy is now. The place to be happy is here. The way to be happy is to make others so'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Robert G. Ingersoll. The exact wording is documented in his 1899 phonograph recording; the kindred thought ends his 1872 lecture “The Gods.”

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Ingersoll. The exact three-sentence wording — including “the place to be happy is here” — is documented in his phonograph recording of 22 January 1899, reported in The Junction City Republican on 3 February 1899. The same thought (without the “here” clause) closes his celebrated 1872 lecture “The Gods” ↗, which is where the closing word “so” comes from — the popular sentence lightly blends his two phrasings, but every clause is his.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Happiness is the only good. The time to be happy is now; the place to be happy is here; and the way to be happy is to make others happy.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to Ingersoll and shows “the place to be happy is here” first appearing in his 1899 phonograph recording.
The two-part thought — “happiness is the only good; that the time to be happy is now, and the way to be happy is to make others so” — closes his 1872 lecture “The Gods” ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the three-part version under Ingersoll in its main sourced quotes.
source.excerptNote: The 1899 recording as reported in The Junction City Republican. The widely-shared version ends “…to make others so,” echoing the close of his 1872 lecture “The Gods.”
source.rightsNote: Ingersoll died in 1899 and both documented sources — his 1872 lecture “The Gods” and the 1899 phonograph recording reported in The Junction City Republican — were published well before 1931, so the wording is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Robert G. Ingersoll
author.heading: About Robert G. Ingersoll
author.metaLine: 1833–1899 · American orator, lawyer & freethinker (‘The Great Agnostic’)
author.bio: Robert Green Ingersoll (1833–1899) was a Civil War veteran, Illinois lawyer, and the most famous American orator of his day, celebrated for spellbinding lectures championing reason, science, and human happiness over religious dogma — earning him the nickname “The Great Agnostic.” His 1872 lecture “The Gods” closes with the creed that happiness is the only good and “the time to be happy is now,” a line he polished across decades of speaking.

misattribution.heading: Set the record straight
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Ingersoll. What’s usually wrong is where people say it comes from, and the exact wording that gets quoted.

items.who: “The Gods” lecture (as the source of the full wording)
items.why: Many sites tie the complete three-part wording to Ingersoll’s 1872 lecture “The Gods” ↗. But that lecture’s peroration has only two of the three clauses — “the time to be happy is now, and the way to be happy is to make others so” — with no “place to be happy is here.”

items.who: “…to make others so” vs. “…to make others happy”
items.why: The circulating sentence blends his two phrasings: the “place to be happy is here” clause comes from his 1899 phonograph recording ↗ (which ends “…make others happy”), while the ending “…make others so” comes from the 1872 lecture.

misattribution.truthLine: Every clause is genuinely Ingersoll’s — but the exact three-sentence wording with “the place to be happy is here” is documented in his 1899 recording ↗, not the 1872 lecture people usually name.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: Ingersoll built this line over nearly thirty years of lecturing. Its earliest form — “happiness is the only good; that the time to be happy is now, and the way to be happy is to make others so” — is the ringing close of his 1872 lecture “The Gods,” his humanist answer to a culture that deferred all reward to the afterlife.

By the time he recorded his voice on an early phonograph in 1899, months before his death, he had added the middle beat — “the place to be happy is here” — giving the creed its now-familiar three-part cadence of now · here · others.
